question:
A 33-year-old African American woman presents to the clinic complaining of pain and swelling of her hands and wrists for the past 5 months. The symptoms are worse in the morning and are associated with stiffness that lasts about 15 minutes. She also complains of profound fatigue and decreased appetite. She is sexually active with one partner in a monogamous relationship. Past medical history is unremarkable and she is taking oral contraceptives. She smokes 1–2 cigarettes per day and drinks alcohol socially on the weekends. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.1°F), blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min, and respirations are 12/min. Physical examination reveals wrists that are tender to palpation, warm, and mildly swollen. Several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints on both hands are also tender. Hand and wrist strength is 5/5 bilaterally. A non-tender ulcer on the buccal mucosa is also noted. When asked about it, the patient reports that it has been there for several months and does not bother her. Laboratory results are as follows:
Complete blood count
Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL
Platelets 90,000/mm3
Leukocytes 6,700/mm3
Blood urea nitrogen 16 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL
Urinalysis
Blood 10–20 red blood cells/hpf
Protein 2+ protein
B-HCG Negative
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Joint pain and swelling in hands and wrists -> Morning stiffness lasting 15 minutes -> Profound fatigue and decreased appetite -> Tender wrists and swollen metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints -> Non-tender ulcer on buccal mucosa -> Laboratory findings: low hemoglobin, low platelets, elevated creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria -> Systemic lupus erythematosus -> 95%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis in this patient is systemic lupus erythematosus. The symptoms of joint pain, swelling, morning stiffness, fatigue, decreased appetite, and laboratory findings of low hemoglobin, low platelets, elevated creatinine, and proteinuria are consistent with SLE. The presence of a non-tender ulcer on the buccal mucosa further supports this diagnosis. Evidence paths linking proteinuria, low platelet count, and decreased hemoglobin to SLE align with the consensus understanding of the disease.
analysis: The core medical principle guiding this diagnosis is the constellation of symptoms including joint pain, swelling, morning stiffness, fatigue, decreased appetite, along with laboratory findings of low hemoglobin, low platelets, elevated creatinine, and proteinuria. The presence of a non-tender ulcer on the buccal mucosa further supports the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). These findings align with the consensus understanding of SLE presentation.
